messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael is a 50-year-old psychologist, married, with a private practice he built over two decades. He sits in the intake session with his hands clasped, his voice steady but hollow. The event that brought him here happened three years ago, at a professional conference in a city he had visited many times. After a day of workshops, he joined colleagues for drinks. He remembers the bar, the low lighting, the smell of someone’s spilled whiskey. He remembers a colleague—someone he trusted—offering to walk him back to his hotel. He remembers nothing after that. The next thing he knows, he is waking in his own room, fully dressed, with a撕裂 feeling in his lower back and a sour taste in his mouth. He has no image of what happened, no sequence of events. His mind simply stops before the memory can complete itself. He has tried, many times, to push through that wall, but each time he feels a physical recoil, as if his brain slams a door shut. The only thing that remains is the emotional truth: a crushing, wordless terror that arrives without warning, sometimes when he is driving, sometimes when he is sitting with a patient, sometimes when he is lying next to his wife at night. He cannot put the event into words because he does not have words for it—only a body that remembers.

In the months afterward, Michael tried to return to his normal life. He is a psychologist; he is supposed to understand trauma. He told himself that the feelings would fade, that he just needed time. But instead, his world began to shrink. The smell of alcohol became unbearable. A colleague’s wine at a dinner party, a patient’s mention of a glass of scotch—his stomach would clench, his throat would close. He stopped attending any social event where drinks might be served. He stopped going to the gym because the locker room sometimes smelled of beer. Sirens became another torment. The first time he heard a siren after the conference, he was in his car and his hands went numb. He pulled over, certain he was having a heart attack. Now he avoids certain streets near the hospital, takes longer routes home, and has started working from home two days a week to reduce his exposure. He told his wife he was tired of the commute.

The most alarming change, to Michael, is what he calls the deadness. He used to be a warm, engaged therapist. He remembered his patients’ details, felt genuine curiosity about their lives. Now he sits across from them and feels nothing—a flat, gray absence. He knows he is nodding, knows he is saying the right things, but he is not there. He has come to believe that he is no longer capable of doing the work that defined him. He thinks, *I am a fraud. I am just going through the motions.* He has started to feel like an object, not a person—something that is looked at, spoken to, but not truly alive. When his wife touches his arm, he feels the pressure but not the warmth. He has stopped initiating sex. He has stopped calling his grown children. He tells himself he is protecting them from his emptiness.

What finally brought Michael to seek help was a moment in his office last week. A patient was describing a panic attack, and Michael suddenly felt the full emotional intensity of his own event—the terror, the helplessness, the shame—without any image, without any memory. He excused himself, went to the bathroom, and wept silently. He realized he could not continue this way. He is terrified that if he lets himself remember, he will shatter. He is equally terrified that he has already shattered, and this deadness is all that is left. He hopes, in some small part of himself he can still reach, that talking might bring him back to life.
